newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House backs bill to aid air crash families.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House backs bill to aid air crash families.

text.p: The House of Representatives voted on Wednesday to create a special family advocate and set guidelines for airlines to follow after disasters, responding to distressing experiences of relatives of plane crash victims.

The bill, passed 401-4, stems from a June hearing in which family members told lawmakers emotional stories of airlines burying body parts of crash victims in mass graves and throwing away personal effects without any prior notification.
Some relatives said they first learned of the death of a loved one through a message left on a telephone answering machine. Others could not get accurate information from airlines.
Emotions flared anew after the still unexplained crash of TWA Flight 800, which plunged into the ocean soon after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport July 17.

"Never again will a family member have to agonize, waiting for information, not knowing where to call or being given abrupt information," said Representative James Oberstar, a Minnesota Democrat, during debate on the measure.

The legislation would require the National Transportation Safety Board to name a family advocate to serve as a bridge between airlines and relatives of crash victims and would bar airlines from disposing of passenger remains and personal effects without consulting family members.
Families would have to be briefed in advance of government news conferences. An independent group, such as the Red Cross, would be designated to coordinate care and support.

Airlines would have to set up a toll-free phone number relatives could call for information, notify families as soon as possible and provide a passenger list to the advocate and Red Cross so that families would have a second place to turn to for information.
Lawyers would be barred from making unsolicited phone calls to family members for 30 days after a crash.

"This legislation will help minimise the suffering of those who lose loved ones in airline tragedies," said Pennsylvania Republican Representative Bud Shuster, chairman of the House Transportation Committee.
The bill must now be considered by the Senate.
